unit.name: Crime, Deviance and Applied Research
unit.subtitle: How crime and deviance are socially constructed, theories of offending, sources of crime data, and how sociologists apply research methods to investigate crime.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat crime and deviance as synonymous. The spec defines them as overlapping but distinct: crime breaks the law; deviance violates social norms (which may or may not be illegal). Some acts are deviant but not criminal (queue-jumping, talking loudly in a library); some are criminal but not seen as widely deviant (minor speeding). Spec section 6.1 explicitly requires students to explain 'social construction of crime and deviance'.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification, section 6.1 — 'social construction of concepts of crime and deviance'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Sociological perspectives confused with each other
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students collapse functionalism and consensus, and Marxism and any conflict view. Each has a precise position: functionalism = society as an integrated whole, institutions perform necessary functions; Marxism = society as class conflict between bourgeoisie and proletariat; feminism = society as patriarchal; interactionism = micro-level meanings, labels and interactions. The spec lists these four and requires students to compare and contrast them on every topic.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification, recurring framing 'conflict versus consensus debate' across sections 2.4, 3.1, 5.1, 6.4.

common_misconceptions.topic: Common-sense answers instead of sociological terminology
common_misconceptions.misconception: Examiner reports flag this as the single biggest discriminator between bands. Students write 'rich people don't get caught' instead of 'differential enforcement of the law'; 'girls behave better' instead of 'patriarchal control of women'. Generic synonyms cap an answer below the sociological-terminology mark band even if the substance is correct.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Sociology Examiners' Report Summer 2024 (eduqas.co.uk/media/ocvnygux/eduqas-gcse-sociology-final-report-s24-e.pdf) — 'Less successful answers were more commonsense in style and lacked the accurate use of terminology'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Hidden curriculum confused with the formal curriculum
common_misconceptions.misconception: The 2024 Component 1 question 5c on the hidden curriculum was a low-scoring item. Students described what schools teach (subjects on the timetable) instead of the unwritten lessons of obedience, hierarchy, punctuality and gender norms transmitted alongside academic content. The spec names hidden curriculum in 3.2 — students must define it as the implicit, informal lessons, link to Bowles and Gintis correspondence theory, and give concrete examples.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Sociology Examiners' Report Summer 2024 (eduqas.co.uk/media/ocvnygux/eduqas-gcse-sociology-final-report-s24-e.pdf) — Component 1 question 5c challenge flagged.

common_misconceptions.topic: Studies attributed to the wrong sociologist
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students confuse the named pairings: Parsons = primary socialisation; Oakley = conventional family; Willmott and Young = symmetrical family; Bowles and Gintis = correspondence principle; Willis = counter school cultures; Becker = labelling; Merton = anomie; Heidensohn = female conformity; Cohen = delinquent subcultures; Carlen = women, crime and poverty; Davis and Moore = functionalist stratification; Townsend = relative deprivation; Murray = underclass; Walby = patriarchy; Chambliss = differential law enforcement; Hargreaves = labelling in classrooms; Becky Francis = patriarchal schools; Devine = affluent worker; Rapoports = five types of diversity; Zaretsky = Marxist family; Delphy and Leonard = patriarchal family.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification — named theorist pairings throughout sections 2-6.

common_misconceptions.topic: Functionalists confused with conservatives on power and inequality
common_misconceptions.misconception: The 2024 examiner report noted: 'Stronger candidates were able to identify that Functionalists accept that there are power differences in society, but that these are inevitable and necessary.' Weaker students assume functionalists deny inequality exists. The Davis and Moore position is that stratification is FUNCTIONAL — necessary, not invisible.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Sociology Examiners' Report Summer 2024 (eduqas.co.uk/media/ocvnygux/eduqas-gcse-sociology-final-report-s24-e.pdf) — explicit comment on the functionalist position on power.

common_misconceptions.topic: Official statistics treated as objective truth
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students cite police-recorded crime figures or divorce statistics as definitive. The spec is explicit: official statistics have strengths AND weaknesses (4.1, 6.5). The dark figure of crime (6.5) is the spec's worked example of why official statistics under-represent crime. Always evaluate, don't just cite.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification, sections 4.1 (sources of secondary data) and 6.5 (dark figure of crime, usefulness of data).

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat 'poverty' as one concept. The spec needs the distinction — absolute (lacking resources for basic survival) vs relative (lacking what is normal in a given society). Townsend's relative deprivation (5.5) includes social participation, not just material need.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification, section 5.5 — 'absolute and relative poverty, including the work of Townsend on relative deprivation'.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students mis-allocate examples to Weber's three types: traditional = legitimacy from custom (monarchy); charismatic = legitimacy from personal qualities (a magnetic political leader); rational-legal = legitimacy from formal rules and offices (an elected MP, a judge). Students often call any leader 'charismatic' and mis-tag elected officials as 'traditional'.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification, section 5.2 — 'Weberian theory of authority: traditional, charismatic and rational-legal'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Medical and social models of disability collapsed into one
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students describe disability as a single concept. The spec (5.3) demands the binary: medical model = disability is the impairment in the individual; social model = disability is created by societal barriers. Students must give one example of each (e.g. medical model: a wheelchair user is 'disabled' by their inability to walk; social model: a wheelchair user is 'disabled' by the absence of ramps).
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification, section 5.3 — 'with specific reference to disability: medical and social models of disability'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Methods evaluation reduced to a generic list
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students recite generic strengths and weaknesses of methods without applying them to a specific research context. The spec explicitly demands evaluation IN CONTEXT. A 12-mark methods Evaluate question expects 'why participant observation is risky for studying gangs specifically', not 'observation is time-consuming' in general.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification, section 4.2 — 'value, practical application and strengths and weaknesses of different methods'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Ethical issues treated as a checklist
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students list 'consent, confidentiality, harm' as boxes to tick rather than reasoning about which apply in a given study and how researchers address them. The spec explicitly requires 'strategies used by sociologists to address issues' (4.5) — students must propose practical solutions (anonymisation, debriefing, withdrawal rights), not just name the principle.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification, section 4.5 — 'strategies used by sociologists to address issues'.

student_errors_by_question_type.1 mark — Multiple Choice: Students leave items blank or guess without reading all four options. With 100 marks per paper, a single multiple choice mark is non-trivial. Read every distractor — plausible-sounding wrong answers are deliberately included to catch confusion of named sociologists or perspectives.
student_errors_by_question_type.2 marks — Define: Students give an example instead of a definition. A 'Define' question expects a meaning expressed in sociological language — 'patriarchy' is 'a system in which men hold power and women are disadvantaged', not 'when men are in charge of the family'. Each mark usually = one element of the definition.
student_errors_by_question_type.3 marks — Identify and Describe: Students identify a feature but fail to describe it. The structure expected is identify (1 mark) plus a developed description (2 marks). Two short sentences score lower than one developed point with sociological vocabulary.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Describe: Students describe one feature when 4 marks usually requires either two developed points or four discrete features. Linking to a named sociologist or concept lifts the answer into the higher mark band.
student_errors_by_question_type.9 marks — Discuss: Students give a one-sided answer or list points without judgement. 2024 examiner report is explicit: 'A common theme on these 9-mark questions is the need to evaluate and analyse.' Top answers present at least two perspectives by name and reach a supported conclusion.
student_errors_by_question_type.12 marks — Evaluate: Students recite knowledge without judgement. The 12-mark Evaluate is the most heavily AO3-weighted question. Top-band answers compare and contrast at least two named perspectives, cite at least two named sociologists, weigh evidence on each side, and arrive at a reasoned conclusion. AO3 is 20% of the qualification — students who skip evaluation cap below grade 7.

topic_weighting_notes: Two papers, 100 marks each, 50% of GCSE each. Component 1 = Cultural Transmission + Families + Education + Research Methods. Component 2 = Stratification + Crime & Deviance + Applied Methods of Sociological Enquiry. Equal weighting forces equal revision time. (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification section 2.)

AO weighting is AO1 40%, AO2 40%, AO3 20% — same per component. Students often overweight AO1 (recall) at the expense of AO2 (application) and AO3 (evaluation). The 9-mark and 12-mark extended response questions are where AO3 is awarded — extended-response practice is non-negotiable. (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification section 3.1.)

A minimum of 15% of the available marks in each examination series is awarded for knowledge and understanding in relation to Research Methods. This is a STANDING REQUIREMENT — research methods will appear on every paper, every year. Drill methods in topic context (methods on family research, methods on crime research). (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification section 3.1.)

Component 2 contains a separate 'Applied Methods of Sociological Enquiry' strand (topic 7) that overlaps with research methods (topic 4) but is assessed differently — the applied strand demands students DESIGN a study and INTERPRET data, not just describe methods. Allocate revision time to scenario-led applied-methods practice, distinct from method-by-method drilling. (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification section 2.2.)

Spec content is set in a UK context except where otherwise stated. UK-relevant examples (Crime Survey for England and Wales, ONS divorce statistics, UK education policy) are expected. Global examples are appropriate where the spec invites them — family forms (2.1, including 'one-child family policy in China', polygamy, arranged marriage) and 'impact of globalisation' on poverty (5.5). (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification section 2 'study the content in a UK context except where otherwise stated'.)

Welsh-context note for WJEC variant: while the specifications are byte-identical, WJEC students sit in Wales. UK-wide examples remain valid for both. Where examples are genuinely English-only (English/Welsh divorce reform 2022 timing, Welsh policy on academies/free schools differing from England's), note jurisdictional scope explicitly without making it a board-specific statement. Lessons stay neutrally phrased.
current_spec_changes: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology has been taught from September 2017, first awarded 2019, and has been in steady state since. Current published version is Version 2 January 2019. No spec content changes are scheduled for 2026 exams. (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification cover page.)

Examination timetable for Summer 2026 is published by WJEC; the qualification is linear (all assessment at the end of the course, in the same series). (Source: WJEC and Eduqas Summer 2026 examination timetable, wjec.co.uk/media/ovdbnkhj/summer-2026-wales-and-eduqas-gcse-october-2025.pdf.)
The qualification is linear and contains no controlled assessment or coursework component. (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification section 4.)

The 2024 examiner report flagged Component 1 question 5c (hidden curriculum) as the lowest-scoring item, with most candidates struggling to define hidden curriculum precisely. Future builds should foreground this concept in the education unit. (Source: Eduqas GCSE Sociology Examiners' Report Summer 2024.)
pedagogical_notes: EEF Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools — disciplinary literacy is critical. Sociology has dense specialist vocabulary. Teach a focused 6-8 term glossary at the start of every lesson and require precise use in extended responses. The 2024 examiner report explicitly flagged that 'less successful answers were more commonsense in style and lacked the accurate use of terminology' — generic synonyms cost marks. (Source: EEF Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools guidance report; Eduqas Examiners' Report Summer 2024.)

EEF Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning (effect size +8 months) — explicitly model how to structure a 9-mark Discuss or 12-mark Evaluate response: argument for (cite a perspective and a named study), argument against (cite a contrasting perspective and study), supported judgement. Students do not do this automatically. Use shared-write worked examples before independent practice. (Source: EEF Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning Guidance Report.)

Retrieval practice — the named sociologists and their key ideas form a finite list of about 20 pairings. Short, frequent low-stakes retrieval quizzes (study + concept + perspective) outperform single long revision sessions. Each lesson ends with a 5-question knowledge check for this reason. (Source: EEF Teaching and Learning Toolkit.)

Compare-and-contrast as a teaching frame — every spec topic asks students to compare perspectives. Build every lesson around a 4-column perspective grid (functionalist / Marxist / feminist / interactionist or New Right where relevant). Students who internalise the grid have an instant scaffold for any 12-mark Evaluate question. (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification — recurring 'conflict versus consensus debate' framing across topics.)

Dual coding — pair every named sociologist with a labelled visual (Bowles and Gintis = school-to-workplace flow diagram showing the correspondence principle; Walby = the six structures of patriarchy as a hexagon). Pair the visual with a one-sentence verbal summary. Ask students to reproduce both halves from memory. (Source: EEF Teaching and Learning Toolkit.)

Sensitive topic handling — sociology covers contested issues (gender roles, ethnic inequality, family diversity, crime, religion, sexuality, disability). Present each as legitimate disagreement between named perspectives rather than as a single authorial line. Treat New Right, Marxist and feminist views with equal descriptive seriousness. This protects the impartiality required by the spec's debate-and-evaluate brief and supports DfE political-impartiality framework. (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification section 1.1 'critically analyse information and use evidence to make informed arguments'; DfE Political impartiality in schools guidance 2022.)

Application as comprehension — many extended response questions are stem-led, presenting an extract or item that students must respond to. Train students to read the stem TWICE: once for content, once for the perspective hooks the examiner has signalled. Every paragraph in the response should reference the stem at least once. (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification — 'reading and responding to extracts which illustrate the different views of sociologists'.)

Data interpretation as a discrete skill — Eduqas/WJEC topic 7.2 explicitly demands students interpret graphs, charts and tables. This is a unique requirement vs other boards. Practise reading data BEFORE moving to causes — present one set of attainment-gap data without explanation, get students to describe the pattern, only then explain. Mirrors the spec separation of patterns (3.3, 6.3) from factors (3.4-3.5, 6.4). (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification sections 7.1, 7.2.)

Examiner-flagged concept: hidden curriculum. 2024 Component 1 5c was the lowest-scoring item — students confused hidden with formal curriculum. Future cohorts must drill the definition (unwritten, implicit lessons of conformity, hierarchy, punctuality, gender norms) and the named link to Bowles and Gintis correspondence theory. (Source: Eduqas GCSE Sociology Examiners' Report Summer 2024.)

_source_meta.source_lesson_title: The Social Construction of Crime and Deviance

source.content_html:
Crime and Deviance: Two Distinct Concepts

One of the first distinctions sociology asks you to make is between crime and deviance. These concepts overlap but are not the same thing. A crime is an act that breaks the formal law; deviance is any behaviour that violates the unwritten social norms of a group or society. Many deviant acts are not criminal — queue-jumping, belching loudly in a restaurant or wearing a swimsuit to a funeral all break social expectations but carry no legal penalty. Equally, some criminal acts are not widely regarded as deviant — many motorists who exceed the speed limit by a small amount do not consider themselves “criminals” in any meaningful social sense.

This distinction matters because sociology treats both crime and deviance as social constructs — they are not fixed, objective categories but are defined and redefined by societies, institutions and individuals over time.

Key Fact

Crime and deviance are related but distinct: crime breaks the formal law; deviance violates social norms. Some acts are only one of these; only some are both. Sociology studies both as social constructs that change across time, place and situation.

Formal and Informal Rules

Societies regulate behaviour through two types of rules. Formal rules are codified in law and backed by state sanctions: fines, imprisonment or community service. Informal rules — sometimes called social norms — govern everyday behaviour through informal pressure: social disapproval, ridicule or exclusion from the group. A student who arrives late to every lesson is breaking an informal norm; a student who commits fraud is breaking a formal rule. Both are forms of deviance in the sociological sense, but only the second is a crime.

Societies use sanctions to enforce both types of rules. Positive sanctions reward conformity (a round of applause, a pay rise, social praise); negative sanctions punish deviation (a fine, a prison sentence, social exclusion). The relationship between formal law and informal norms is itself a sociological question: laws tend to reflect the norms of the dominant groups in society, a point Marxist and feminist perspectives challenge.

The Relativity of Deviance

A key insight of sociology is that deviance is relative: what counts as deviant varies across time, place and social situation. Three dimensions of relativity are particularly important.

Across time: Acts that were once legal can become criminal — fox hunting with dogs was a lawful rural tradition in England and Wales until the Hunting Act 2004 made it a criminal offence. Conversely, acts once treated as crimes can be decriminalised or legalised — homosexual acts between consenting adult men were criminal offences in England and Wales until the Sexual Offences Act 1967 partially decriminalised them. The law changes as the values and power structures of society change.

Across place: The same act may be legal in one country but criminal in another. Cannabis possession is legal for recreational use in the Netherlands under certain conditions but remains a criminal offence in England and Wales. Drinking alcohol in a public place is unremarkable in most of the United Kingdom but constitutes a serious offence in countries that enforce strict religious law. These cross-cultural variations demonstrate that crime is not an inherent property of an act but a label applied by a society.

Across situation: Context shapes whether an act is considered deviant. Killing another person is treated as murder in most contexts but may be regarded as heroic in warfare, or legally permitted as self-defence. A surgeon cutting open a patient's body with a scalpel is performing a legitimate medical procedure; the same action outside that context would be an assault. Interactionist sociologists like Becker emphasised that deviance is not a quality of the act itself but is created by the reactions of audiences to the act.

Sociological Perspectives on the Social Construction of Crime

Different sociological perspectives explain the social construction of crime in contrasting ways, reflecting deeper disagreements about the nature of society.

A very common examination error is to treat crime and deviance as synonyms. They are overlapping but distinct categories. The simplest way to keep them separate is to think of two overlapping circles: the left circle is all criminal acts, the right circle is all deviant acts. The overlap in the middle is acts that are both criminal and widely seen as deviant (such as violent assault). The left-only region is acts that are criminal but not seen as deviant by most people (minor speeding). The right-only region is acts that are deviant but not criminal (being rude to a stranger). On an exam question asking you to “define deviance”, giving a legal definition will lose marks.

Functionalist perspective: From a functionalist viewpoint, crime and deviance are defined relative to the value consensus of society. Durkheim argued that some level of crime is normal and even functional in any society — it helps clarify the boundaries of acceptable behaviour and, when punished, reaffirms shared values. On this view, defining something as “criminal” is the community expressing its moral boundaries.

Marxist perspective: Marxist sociologists argue that criminal law is not a neutral reflection of shared values but an instrument of class power. The bourgeoisie shape the law to protect their property and interests, criminalising acts common among the working class (street theft) while failing to criminalise or leniently treating harmful acts by the powerful (corporate fraud, tax evasion). The social construction of “crime” therefore reflects and reinforces class inequality.

Feminist perspective: Feminist sociologists point out that laws have historically been made predominantly by men and have often reflected patriarchal interests. Many acts of violence against women — marital rape, for instance — were not defined as criminal in England and Wales until relatively recently (rape within marriage was only conclusively criminalised in R v R, 1991). Definitions of crime and deviance therefore embed gender power relations, and feminist research examines how the social construction of crime affects women both as victims and as offenders.

Interactionist perspective: Interactionists such as Becker argue that no act is inherently criminal or deviant; it becomes so only when a label is successfully applied to it by someone with the power to make the label stick. The social construction of crime is an ongoing process of labelling, negotiation and reaction. Becker used the term moral entrepreneurs to describe individuals and groups who actively campaign for certain behaviours to be defined as deviant or criminal — pressure groups lobbying for new legislation are a contemporary example.

Key Fact

Four perspectives explain social construction differently: functionalists see crime as defined by shared values; Marxists see law as serving the ruling class; feminists see law as historically shaped by patriarchal power; interactionists focus on labelling as the mechanism by which acts become “criminal” or “deviant”.

Law and Morality: Are They the Same?

A final dimension of the social construction of crime is the relationship between law and morality. Not everything that is morally condemned is illegal, and not everything that is illegal is morally condemned by all members of society. Lying to a friend is widely regarded as morally wrong but carries no legal penalty. Some individuals regard civil disobedience — breaking an unjust law — as a moral act. The gap between law and morality varies across time and culture and is itself a product of social processes. Sociologists are interested in who gets to define the law, whose morality it encodes, and whose behaviour it criminalises — questions that run through the entire sociology of crime and deviance.
source.exam_tip_html: The command word “Define” asks you to provide a clear sociological meaning for a term — not an example of it. Students often write “deviance is when someone does something that breaks the rules, like stealing” and lose a mark because “like stealing” replaces the definition with an example. A strong definition of deviance would read: “behaviour that violates the social norms of a group or society.” Each mark on a 2-mark Define question typically corresponds to one element of the definition — so adding a qualifying clause (“whether or not it is illegal”) earns the second mark. On the 12-mark Discuss, examiners reward students who present the views of at least two named sociologists or perspectives and reach a supported conclusion. One-sided answers that only present the interactionist view, for example, cannot reach the Mastering tier.

Key Takeaways

  • Crime and deviance are distinct: crime breaks formal law; deviance violates social norms. Many acts are only one of these, not both — this distinction is tested directly in your exam.
  • Both are social constructs: what counts as criminal or deviant varies across time, place and social situation, showing that these categories are created by society rather than fixed by nature.
  • Functionalists, Marxists, feminists and interactionists each offer a different explanation for who defines crime and deviance, and whose interests those definitions serve.

source.content_html:
What Is Social Control?

Social control refers to the range of ways in which societies regulate behaviour and encourage conformity. Without social control, functionalist sociologists argue, social order would break down — the shared norms and values holding society together would lose their binding force. Sociologists identify two broad categories of social control: formal social control and informal social control.

The distinction matters for sociology because different perspectives disagree sharply about whose norms are enforced, who benefits from social control, and whether the mechanisms of control operate fairly across different social groups.

Formal Social Control: The Criminal Justice System

Formal social control is exercised by agencies of formal social control — primarily the police, the courts and the prison system. These agencies are authorised by the state to use legal power to enforce rules and impose formal sanctions on those who break the law.

The police act as the front line of formal control, with powers of stop and search, arrest and detention. However, sociologists note that policing is not neutral: the decision to stop, question or arrest a suspect involves discretion, and research suggests that this discretion can be applied unequally. Interactionist sociologists point out that police stereotypes about who “looks criminal” influence where resources are deployed and who is stopped. Courts determine guilt and impose sentences. Prisons serve multiple stated purposes: punishment, deterrence, rehabilitation and incapacitation (removing offenders from society). Critics of the prison system argue that it disproportionately incarcerates people from disadvantaged social backgrounds and has limited effectiveness as a deterrent.

Functionalist view: The criminal justice system performs a necessary social function. By identifying, prosecuting and punishing offenders, it reinforces the collective moral boundaries of society (Durkheim’s boundary maintenance function). Without formal control, social order would collapse. The police and courts are seen as broadly serving society’s shared interests.

Marxist view: Marxist sociologists argue that formal social control primarily serves the interests of the bourgeoisie. The police and courts direct their attention disproportionately at working-class crime (street theft, disorder, benefit fraud) while largely ignoring or under-penalising the harmful acts of the powerful (corporate crime, tax avoidance, financial fraud). The prison population in England and Wales is drawn overwhelmingly from disadvantaged backgrounds — a pattern that Marxists argue reflects the class-based nature of formal control.

Interactionist view: Formal control involves discretion at every stage — police officers decide who to stop; prosecutors decide who to charge; judges and juries assess credibility. Becker’s labelling theory shows that these discretionary decisions are shaped by stereotypes and social power, not just by the evidence of rule-breaking. The result is selective enforcement that amplifies existing inequalities.

Informal Social Control: Family, Peers, Media and More

Informal social control operates through the everyday expectations, pressures and reactions of social groups rather than through legal authority. Its agencies include the family, the peer group, the school, religion, the media and the workplace. Informal control works primarily through informal sanctions: praise, approval and inclusion on one hand; ridicule, disapproval and social exclusion on the other.

The family: The family is typically the first agency of socialisation and informal control. Parents establish rules, reward conformity and sanction deviance long before formal institutions intervene. The norms children internalise in the family setting — about honesty, aggression, gender behaviour — shape their behaviour in other social contexts. Feminist sociologists note that family-based informal control operates differently for boys and girls: daughters are typically given less freedom of movement, face earlier curfews and are held to different standards of behaviour.

The peer group: As young people grow older, the peer group becomes an increasingly important source of informal control. Peer approval and rejection are powerful motivators: individuals conform to group norms (dress, speech, attitudes, behaviour) to maintain belonging and social status. Subcultural theorists like Cohen argued that peer groups can also exert control in the direction of deviance, where group norms celebrate norm-breaking and where conformity to the wider society’s expectations earns ridicule rather than approval.

Education: Schools exercise informal control through teacher expectations, praise and punishment, the hidden curriculum (embedding norms of punctuality, obedience and effort) and through peer dynamics. The formal rules of schools (uniforms, timetables, detention systems) overlap with informal peer pressure to shape student behaviour.

Religion: Religious institutions and belief systems promote moral codes and community expectations. Fear of social exclusion from a religious community, or internalised religious values, can serve as powerful informal controls. In more secular societies, the direct influence of religion on everyday conformity has arguably declined, though religious values continue to shape family norms.

The media: The media exerts informal control by setting agendas, shaping public norms and rewarding or stigmatising certain behaviours. Media coverage of crime, in particular, can contribute to moral panics that heighten public anxiety and informal social pressure. Advertising and popular culture promote norms of consumption, gender behaviour and lifestyle that function as informal expectations.

Heidensohn: Patriarchal Control and Female Conformity

Frances Heidensohn, in Women and Crime (1985), offered a feminist explanation for one of the most consistent patterns in crime data: women commit far fewer crimes than men. Rather than explaining this through biological difference or individual psychology, Heidensohn argued that women are subject to far more intensive social control than men, making it structurally more difficult for them to deviate.

Heidensohn used patriarchal control theory as her framework. She identified three domains in which women are controlled more tightly than men:

  • Control in the home: Women are expected to spend the majority of their time on domestic labour and childcare. Those who challenge these expectations risk male violence as an assertion of patriarchal authority. Men as the main or sole breadwinner hold financial power that limits women’s independence. Daughters are controlled more strictly than sons — earlier curfews, more restrictions on movement, greater expectations of domestic contribution.
  • Control in public: Women face the threat of male sexual violence in public spaces, which acts as an informal deterrent against independent movement, particularly at night. The cultural idea of “separate spheres” — women’s proper place as the home — means that women who occupy public space conspicuously or in ways that challenge expectations may face ridicule, harassment or judgement.
  • Control at work: Women are controlled by male-dominated hierarchies and subjected to various forms of sexual harassment. Organisational cultures and workers’ organisations have historically been male-dominated, limiting women’s opportunities and autonomy.

Heidensohn’s argument is that women’s lower crime rates are not evidence of superior morality or greater law-abidingness but the result of more intensive control that restricts their opportunities to offend. This connects directly to the broader feminist argument that social life is structured by patriarchy and that gender shapes social experiences in profound ways.

Key Fact

Heidensohn (Women and Crime, 1985) argues that women’s lower crime rates reflect the intensity of patriarchal control they face — in the home (domestic expectations and male violence), in public (threat of sexual violence, separate spheres ideology) and at work (male-dominated hierarchies and harassment).

Key Fact

Formal control uses legal authority (police, courts, prisons) backed by state-imposed sanctions. Informal control uses social pressure and norms (family, peers, media, religion, education) and operates through everyday interaction. Both types can be analysed from functionalist, Marxist, feminist and interactionist perspectives — each asking different questions about who controls, who benefits and who is most controlled.

Heidensohn’s work has been influential but also criticised. She has been challenged for making generalisations that do not apply to all women: the experience of control differs significantly by class, ethnicity, age and location. Her account also focuses on why women do not commit crime, which some argue tells us less about women’s actual offending patterns (particularly as rates of female offending have changed since 1985) than about the exceptional circumstances under which women do offend. Carlen’s later work on women, crime and poverty (1988) added the insight that when the “class deal” and “gender deal” both fail working-class women, crime becomes a rational alternative — extending the feminist account to intersect with class inequality.
source.exam_tip_html: On a 3-mark “Identify and Describe” question about social control, make sure you distinguish between formal and informal control clearly. A common error is to describe the police (formal control) when asked for an example of informal control. Informal control operates through everyday social interaction and does not involve legal authority — the family enforcing a curfew, peers mocking someone for dressing differently, or media coverage setting norms are all informal. On the 12-mark Discuss, Heidensohn is a named sociologist that many students know about but describe too vaguely: be specific about her three domains of control (home, public, work) and link the argument to the broader feminist framework. The Mastering tier expects you to evaluate: a strong answer will consider both supports for Heidensohn’s view and challenges to it (e.g. Carlen on class and gender intersecting, changes in female offending rates since 1985).
source.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Social control operates through two channels: formal control (police, courts, prisons) backed by legal authority, and informal control (family, peers, media, religion) operating through social pressure and norms.
  • Functionalists see both as necessary for social order; Marxists argue both primarily serve ruling-class interests; interactionists focus on how discretion shapes who is controlled; feminists examine how gender shapes both the type and intensity of control.
  • Heidensohn (Women and Crime, 1985) argues that women’s lower crime rates result from more intensive patriarchal control in the home, in public and at work — not from greater inherent conformity or morality.

source.content_html:
Why Do Rates of Crime Vary Across Social Groups?

Sociology asks not just what crime is, but who commits it, and why certain social groups appear in crime statistics more than others. Official figures and self-report studies consistently show that rates of offending are not evenly spread across society. They vary by social class, gender, ethnicity and age. Sociological perspectives disagree sharply about what drives these patterns and what they actually mean.

Key Fact

The four main factors sociologists identify as affecting criminal behaviour are social class, gender, ethnicity and age. Each factor is interpreted differently by functionalist, Marxist, feminist and interactionist perspectives.

Social Class and Crime

Police-recorded crime and self-report studies both suggest that working-class individuals are overrepresented in offending data, particularly for street crime, theft and burglary. However, sociological perspectives explain this in very different ways.

From a functionalist standpoint, Robert Merton’s strain theory argues that crime results from a mismatch between the shared cultural goal of material success and the unequal availability of legitimate means to achieve it. Those with fewer educational qualifications and employment prospects are more likely to turn to “innovation” — using illegal means to achieve socially approved goals. This places working-class individuals at higher risk, but Merton does not treat their criminality as inevitable or biologically determined.

Albert Cohen, writing in Delinquent Boys (1955), developed a subculture theory that extends Merton’s account. Cohen argued that working-class boys share the same success goals as the rest of society, but that educational failure and poor employment prospects leave them unable to achieve those goals through legitimate routes. The resulting status frustration leads them to reject mainstream values and create an alternative status hierarchy within a delinquent subculture. Within that subculture, status is gained through activities such as theft, vandalism and truancy rather than through school or work. A successful thief earns prestige from peers in a way that the school system denies him.

Critics of Cohen point out that not all working-class young people form delinquent subcultures, and that his theory assumes working-class youths internalise mainstream goals in the first place. Some sociologists argue instead that working-class young men may actively reject those goals rather than feel frustrated by failing to achieve them.

Marxist perspectives challenge the focus on working-class crime altogether. They argue that the law is shaped in the interests of the bourgeoisie, meaning that white-collar crime (fraud, tax evasion, corporate harm) committed by more powerful groups attracts less police attention and lighter sentencing. The official statistics therefore exaggerate working-class criminality not because working-class people commit more harm, but because their crimes are more visible and more likely to be prosecuted.

A common error is to treat crime statistics as proving that working-class people are naturally more criminal. Sociologists reject this. Official crime figures record crimes that are reported and prosecuted. Marxists argue that white-collar and corporate crimes cause enormous financial and physical harm (unsafe working conditions, fraudulent financial products) but receive far less police attention. The overrepresentation of working-class individuals in the statistics may reflect policing priorities and legal definitions as much as actual behaviour. Always distinguish the pattern in the data from the explanation for that pattern.

Gender and Crime

Men commit the large majority of recorded crimes in England and Wales. Official figures consistently show that male offenders account for roughly three-quarters of all prosecutions. Sociologists offer several explanations for this gender gap.

Functionalist accounts emphasise gender socialisation: boys are socialised to be tough, assertive and risk-taking, traits that make criminality more likely. Girls are socialised towards conformity, care and domestic roles, making deviance less likely. This explanation treats gender roles as functional for social order.

Frances Heidensohn, writing in Women and Crime (1985) from a feminist perspective, offers a more structural account using control theory. Heidensohn argues that women commit fewer crimes because patriarchal society controls them far more effectively than it controls men. In the home, women are expected to spend their time on housework and childcare; those who challenge these expectations risk male violence as an assertion of patriarchal authority. In public, women are controlled by the threat of sexual violence and the fear that “inappropriate” behaviour will damage their reputation. At work, women face male-dominated hierarchies and sexual harassment. This web of patriarchal control restricts women’s opportunities for deviance far more than equivalent controls restrict men.

Pat Carlen, in Women, Crime and Poverty (1988), studied 39 working-class women who had been convicted of criminal offences, using in-depth unstructured interviews. Carlen also draws on control theory but foregrounds class alongside gender. She argues that women are controlled through two kinds of deal. The class deal promises working-class women consumer goods and a respectable lifestyle in exchange for their labour. The gender deal offers psychological and material rewards through a male breadwinner in exchange for love and domestic labour. When either or both deals break down — through unemployment, poverty or abusive relationships — crime becomes a rational choice because the usual incentives for conformity are absent. Carlen’s work has been critiqued for its small sample size, but it is important because it connects women’s criminality to structural inequality rather than individual pathology.

Ethnicity and Crime

Official statistics show that Black individuals are overrepresented in stop-and-search figures and in prison populations relative to their share of the general population. Sociologists treat this as a pattern requiring critical analysis, not as evidence of inherently higher criminality.

Key Fact

Overrepresentation of ethnic minorities in crime statistics is explained by sociologists through: (1) interactionist labelling and selective policing; (2) Marxist arguments about institutional racism; and (3) structural explanations linking poverty and deprivation to crime rates. No perspective treats the pattern as proof of biological difference.

From an interactionist standpoint, the overrepresentation reflects policing practices rather than offending behaviour. Becker’s labelling theory suggests that the police apply stereotyped labels to young Black men, making them more likely to be stopped and searched, arrested and charged. The label “criminal” then becomes a master status that shapes how the individual is treated by courts and employers, increasing the risk of further offending through a self-fulfilling prophecy.

A Marxist perspective connects racial inequality in the criminal justice system to wider structural inequalities. Ethnic minorities are disproportionately represented among those in poverty and those in low-paid, insecure employment. If crime is partly driven by material deprivation, then economic marginalisation explains some of the overrepresentation. Additionally, Marxists point to institutional racism in policing and the courts as reproducing racial inequality through the criminal justice system itself.

Examining patterns in crime data by ethnicity is a legitimate and important sociological task, but it requires critical awareness. The Macpherson Report (1999) into the Metropolitan Police’s handling of Stephen Lawrence’s murder concluded that the force was “institutionally racist”, giving a UK context to the interactionist and Marxist arguments above. Sociologists consistently emphasise that the data shows overrepresentation in police-recorded outcomes — which reflect policing choices — and that stop-and-search rates cannot be used as straightforward evidence of higher offending. Any analysis should name the mechanisms being proposed (selective policing, institutional racism, material deprivation) rather than leaving the pattern unexplained.

Age and Crime

Crime data consistently shows that offending peaks in late adolescence and early adulthood, with the highest rates among those aged 15 to 24. Sociological explanations draw on both structural and interactionist factors. From a functionalist perspective, young people may have less stake in conformity — they are less likely to own property, hold stable employment or have family responsibilities that make law-abiding behaviour rewarding. Cohen’s delinquent subculture theory is particularly relevant here, as it focuses specifically on young working-class men. From an interactionist standpoint, young people are more likely to be subject to police surveillance and labelling, which inflates their recorded crime rates beyond their actual offending.
source.exam_tip_html: The 12-mark Discuss question on factors affecting criminal behaviour often asks you to assess one factor, such as social class or gender, and invite you to weigh competing perspectives. A common error is to describe only one perspective (for example, only Merton’s strain theory) without considering others. To reach the Mastering tier, you must present arguments from at least two perspectives — for example, Merton’s functionalist explanation alongside Carlen’s feminist account or a Marxist argument about selective enforcement — develop each with a named sociologist, and reach a supported judgement. A well-structured answer might conclude that class is a partial explanation but must be read alongside gender and policing patterns, since the crime statistics themselves are socially produced. Remember: recall of the named studies (Albert Cohen, Carlen) earns recall marks, but evaluation of competing perspectives is what lifts the response into the top band.
source.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Four key factors shape patterns of criminal behaviour in official statistics: social class, gender, ethnicity and age. Each factor is explained differently by functionalist, Marxist, feminist and interactionist perspectives.
  • Albert Cohen (Delinquent Boys, 1955) argued that working-class boys experience status frustration due to educational failure, and form delinquent subcultures with an alternative status hierarchy. Carlen (Women, Crime and Poverty, 1988) argued that women turn to crime when the class deal and gender deal break down.
  • Overrepresentation of ethnic minorities in crime statistics requires critical analysis: interactionist and Marxist perspectives point to selective policing, labelling and institutional racism as factors that inflate the figures rather than reflecting higher actual offending rates.

source.content_html:
Durkheim: Crime Is Normal and Functional

Functionalist sociology begins from the premise that society works like a living organism: its institutions perform necessary functions and, when working well, produce social order and value consensus. Emile Durkheim argued that crime is not simply a social problem to be eliminated — it is a normal feature of every known society. If crime were to disappear entirely, Durkheim reasoned, society would have become so rigid and repressive that even the most minor non-conformity would be treated as a serious offence. A healthy society requires a certain level of deviance to function.

Durkheim identified two functions of crime. First, crime performs a boundary maintenance function: when an offender is publicly punished, the community gathers around the shared moral boundary that has been violated, reaffirming collective values. Court proceedings, media coverage of verdicts and public discussion of serious crimes all serve this ritual function. Second, crime can act as a driver of social change: acts that are initially labelled criminal — civil rights protests, for example — may eventually prompt a rethinking of the law. Yesterday’s criminal can become tomorrow’s reformer.

Durkheim also introduced the concept of anomie — a state of normlessness that arises when the rules holding society together break down. For Durkheim, periods of rapid social change (economic booms or slumps) could weaken the norms that regulate individual desires, leading to an increase in deviant behaviour. Robert Merton later developed this concept into a full theory of crime.

Key Fact

Durkheim argued crime performs two functions for society: boundary maintenance (reaffirming shared values through punishment) and enabling social change (challenging unjust laws). He also introduced anomie — normlessness resulting from the breakdown of social rules.

Merton: Strain Theory and the Goals–Means Gap

Robert Merton, writing in Social Theory and Social Structure (1938, enlarged 1968), developed Durkheim’s concept of anomie into a systematic theory of crime. Merton argued that deviance results from the culture and structure of society — not from individual pathology or moral failure.

Merton started from the functionalist premise of value consensus: all members of society are socialised into the same cultural goals, particularly the goal of material success. However, because members of society have different positions in the social structure, they do not have equal access to the institutionalised means — the legitimate routes (education, employment, talent) through which success is achieved. Members of the working class and poor communities are socialised into the same aspirations as everyone else but face far greater structural barriers to achieving them.

This gap between cultural goals and institutionalised means creates a strain that puts pressure on individuals to deviate. Crucially, Merton believed that in American society (the context of his original research, though his ideas have wide application) the emphasis on success far outweighed the emphasis on achieving it legitimately — “winning at all costs” encouraged a state of anomie in which the usual rules governing behaviour were abandoned. The concept can be applied in a UK context: the expectation of consumer lifestyle success is widely promoted through media and advertising, yet structural barriers (class inequality, educational inequalities) mean that not all routes to that success are equally available.

Merton’s Five Responses to Strain

Merton identified five ways in which individuals can respond to the tension between cultural goals and the available means to achieve them. These are not personality types but modes of adaptation to social structure.

1. Conformity: Accepts both the cultural goals (material success) and the institutionalised means (education, employment). This is the most common adaptation and produces social stability. The conformist works hard, gains qualifications and pursues a career within the rules of the system.

2. Innovation: Accepts the cultural goals but rejects or lacks access to the legitimate means. The individual turns instead to deviant or criminal methods — theft, fraud, drug dealing. Merton argued that innovation was most common among those lower in the class structure who faced the greatest gap between aspirations and opportunities. This is the response most directly linked to crime.

3. Ritualism: Rejects or abandons the cultural goals (no longer striving for wealth and success) but continues to follow the institutionalised means rigidly. The ritualist remains in a low-paid, low-status job and follows the rules to the letter — perhaps through an enthusiasm for petty bureaucracy — without expecting advancement. Merton associated this with some middle-class individuals who have been strongly socialised to conform but have little prospect of upward mobility.

4. Retreatism: Rejects both the cultural goals and the means of achieving them. The retreatist “drops out” of society altogether, withdrawing from mainstream life. Merton applied this concept to explain the behaviour of people experiencing chronic poverty, homelessness or long-term addiction. This adaptation involves neither conventional success nor criminal gain — simply withdrawal.

5. Rebellion: Rejects both existing cultural goals and means but replaces them with alternative goals and means. Unlike the retreatist, the rebel acts to create a new social order. Merton saw this as typical of members of a “rising class” who may attempt organised political revolt or social revolution.

Key Fact

Merton’s five responses: Conformity (accepts goals + means), Innovation (accepts goals, rejects means — most linked to crime), Ritualism (rejects goals, accepts means), Retreatism (rejects both), Rebellion (rejects both, substitutes new goals and means).

Subcultural Theories: Albert Cohen

Albert Cohen, in Delinquent Boys (1955), extended the strain tradition but shifted focus from individual adaptation to collective, subcultural responses. Cohen argued that working-class boys hold the same success goals as the wider society but, because of cultural deprivation and poor educational prospects, they consistently fail to achieve by mainstream standards.

This failure produces what Cohen called status frustration. Rather than innovating individually (Merton’s route), working-class boys respond collectively by forming delinquent subcultures that invert the mainstream values they have been denied: they celebrate vandalism, truancy and theft not because these acts gain material wealth but because they gain status and prestige within the subculture. Success at what the mainstream condemns becomes a source of peer recognition.

Cohen’s approach adds an important dimension missing from Merton’s theory: it explains non-instrumental crime — acts committed not for economic gain but for status, thrill or group belonging. Critics of Cohen argue that not all working-class boys experience school failure in the same way, and that his account overlooks girls and young women entirely. Feminist and interactionist perspectives offer different explanations for why subcultures form along gendered lines.

Evaluating Functionalist and Subcultural Theories

Merton’s strain theory has been influential because it shifts blame for crime from individuals to the social structure. However, critics point out several limitations. Marxist sociologists argue that Merton fails to ask who makes the laws and who benefits from them: focusing on working-class innovation ignores corporate crime, tax evasion and white-collar offending. Interactionist critics argue that Merton assumes a single value system (success goals) shared by all, when in practice values vary across class, gender and ethnicity. Feminist critics note that Merton’s theory is largely silent on women and crime. Cohen has been criticised for overstating cultural deprivation as the cause of working-class failure and for producing an account that applies only to young males in urban settings.

Students sometimes write “anomie means crime.” Anomie is the condition — a state of normlessness or the breakdown of social rules — not the criminal behaviour itself. Crime (specifically innovation in Merton’s framework) is one possible response to anomie, but conformity, retreatism and other adaptations are also responses to the same condition. Always define anomie as normlessness or the breakdown of rules, then explain how it can lead to deviance.
source.exam_tip_html: On a 4-mark Describe question about Merton, students often list only two or three of his five responses when the question asks for two developed descriptions. Each of the five responses should be described in terms of the combination it makes: accepting or rejecting (a) the cultural goals and (b) the institutionalised means. If you can’t remember all five in an exam, prioritise Conformity (both accepted), Innovation (goals accepted, means rejected — most directly crime-linked) and Retreatism (both rejected). For the 12-mark Discuss, the strongest answers will contrast Merton’s structural explanation with at least one other perspective — for example, the Marxist critique that strain theory ignores corporate crime, or the interactionist critique that not everyone shares the same success goals. A supported judgement at the end is essential for the Mastering tier.
source.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Durkheim argued crime is normal and functional: it maintains social boundaries and can drive social change. Anomie describes the normlessness that arises when social rules break down.
  • Merton’s strain theory explains crime as a structural response to the gap between shared cultural goals (success) and unequal access to legitimate means. His five adaptations are: Conformity, Innovation, Ritualism, Retreatism and Rebellion.
  • Albert Cohen extended strain theory into subcultural theory: working-class boys experiencing status frustration form delinquent subcultures that invert mainstream values. Critics of both Merton and Cohen argue their theories neglect women, white-collar crime and the role of labelling.

source.content_html:
The Interactionist Challenge

Functionalist and structural theories ask why certain social conditions (strain, status frustration, class inequality) lead to crime. Interactionist sociology asks a different question: who decides what counts as criminal or deviant in the first place, and what happens to individuals once they are labelled? This shift of focus — from the causes of rule-breaking to the social processes of labelling — produced one of the most influential perspectives in the sociology of crime.

Interactionism argues that social reality is constructed through interaction and the meanings people assign to actions. Applied to crime and deviance, this means that an act has no inherent criminal quality — it becomes deviant only when someone with the power to make the label stick successfully defines it as such.

Becker: Labelling Theory

Howard Becker, in Outsiders (1963), set out the foundational argument of labelling theory. Becker argued that deviance is not a property of the act itself but of the interaction between the person who acts and those who observe and respond to the act. Whether a label of “deviant” or “criminal” is applied depends on who commits the act, when and where it is committed, who observes it, and the negotiations between the various parties involved.

Becker observed that not all rule-breakers are caught, and not all who are caught are labelled. Whether a label sticks depends on factors beyond the act itself: the social characteristics of the actor (class, ethnicity, age, gender), the discretion of those with formal power (police, teachers, courts), and the social context. Two young people committing the same act may receive very different responses depending on where they are and who they are. Becker’s insight was that the criminal justice system is not a neutral machine but a social process shaped by power.

Key Fact

Becker (Outsiders, 1963) argued that deviance is not a property of the act but is created by the reactions of others. An act only becomes deviant when a label is successfully applied by someone with the power to make it stick.

Master Status and the Deviant Career

Once a label has been publicly and officially applied, Becker argued, it tends to become the person’s master status. Before the label, a young person might be seen as a student, a friend, a neighbour. After being officially convicted and labelled a “criminal”, this identity overshadows all others. Assumptions are made about the person’s character, reliability and likely future behaviour — assumptions that can follow them into every interaction: with employers, with landlords, with teachers, with family members.

The consequences of master status may trigger what Becker described as a deviant career. As the labelled individual is rejected from legitimate social roles — turned down by employers, excluded from educational opportunities, cut off from conventional social networks — the label itself makes conventional life harder to sustain. This rejection can produce a self-fulfilling prophecy: the individual increasingly identifies with the label and seeks out others who share it, joining organised deviant groups with their own norms, values and identity. In this way, the labelling process can transform an isolated act of rule-breaking into an ongoing criminal lifestyle — not because the individual was inevitably going to become a criminal, but because the social reaction created the conditions for it.

Primary and Secondary Deviance

Primary deviance refers to the original act of rule-breaking, before any label has been applied. Most people commit acts of primary deviance at some point (minor theft, underage drinking, breaking traffic rules) without it becoming part of their identity. Secondary deviance occurs when an individual internalises the deviant label and begins to act in accordance with it. The distinction is important: the theory argues that secondary deviance is produced not by the original act but by the social reaction to it.

Moral Entrepreneurs and Moral Panics

Becker also introduced the concept of moral entrepreneurs — individuals and groups who use their social influence to get particular behaviours defined as deviant. They may lobby parliament for new legislation, campaign in the media, or pressure institutions to act. Their success depends on their social power and their ability to frame the issue in ways that resonate with public anxieties.

Related to this is the concept of a moral panic. When the media, police and public respond to a perceived threat in a disproportionate and amplified way, the resulting attention can itself increase the visible scale of the problem through a process of deviancy amplification: increased police attention leads to more arrests, which generates more media coverage, which fuels further anxiety and policing. The labelling process escalates. Critics argue that moral panics have historically targeted specific groups (young working-class men, ethnic minority communities) who are portrayed as “folk devils” — symbols of social threat.

Feminist perspective: Feminist sociologists broadly welcome the insight that labelling is not neutral. Heidensohn noted that the criminal justice system has historically applied labels differently to men and women: women offenders are sometimes treated more leniently (the “chivalry thesis”) when they conform to feminine stereotypes, but women who deviate from expected gender roles may be judged more harshly. Feminist criminologists argue that the identity of the label-appliers — predominantly male judges, police and juries — shapes who is targeted and how they are treated.

Marxist perspective: Marxist sociologists argue that labelling theory does not go far enough because it focuses on individual interactions without asking why the police and courts are more likely to label working-class people as criminal. The answer, for Marxists, lies in the class structure: the bourgeoisie controls the legal system and ensures that the label “criminal” is attached primarily to acts associated with the proletariat (street crime, theft, benefit fraud) rather than to the far more costly but largely tolerated crimes of the powerful (corporate fraud, tax avoidance, environmental damage). Selective law enforcement reflects and reinforces class inequality.

Key Fact

Labelling theory has been criticised from multiple directions: Marxists argue it doesn’t explain why labels fall on the working class (class power); feminists argue gender shapes both labelling and its consequences; critics also note that not everyone who is labelled accepts or acts on the label (determinism).

Strengths: Labelling theory challenges the view that crime statistics are an objective reflection of criminal behaviour, showing instead that they reflect the activities of the police and courts. It draws attention to the unequal application of labels across social groups. It helps explain patterns such as recidivism (re-offending after conviction), which purely structural theories struggle to account for.

Weaknesses: Labelling theory has been criticised for being too deterministic — not everyone who is labelled becomes a career criminal; many labelled individuals resist and reject the identity. It focuses on the label-givers (police, courts) but underplays the role of the actor’s own choices and motivations. Functionalists argue that labelling theory cannot explain why some acts (serious violence) are universally condemned regardless of the social identity of the actor.

A strong 4-mark answer needs both: the process of labelling (who applies labels, under what conditions) and its consequences (master status reshapes how others respond; self-fulfilling prophecy reshapes the individual’s own identity). For the 12-mark Discuss, the highest-scoring answers will compare labelling theory with at least one other perspective — e.g. contrasting Becker’s focus on the reaction of others with Merton’s focus on structural strain, or with the Marxist point that labelling reflects class power. Always end with a supported judgement that weighs the evidence.
source.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Becker’s labelling theory (Outsiders, 1963) argues that deviance is not a quality of the act but is created by the social reaction to it. An act becomes deviant when a powerful audience successfully labels it as such.
  • Once labelled, a person may acquire a master status that overrides all other identities, triggering a deviant career through the self-fulfilling prophecy as they are excluded from conventional roles and drawn into organised deviant groups.
  • Marxists and feminists extend labelling theory: Marxists argue class power determines who gets labelled; feminists argue gender shapes both who is targeted and how they are treated. Both perspectives challenge the interactionist focus on individual interaction without addressing structural inequality.

source.content_html:
What Do We Actually Know About Crime?

Before sociologists can analyse crime, they must grapple with a fundamental methodological question: how is crime measured, and how reliable are those measurements? Different sources of crime data paint different pictures, and sociological perspectives disagree about what official statistics reveal, conceal and distort. This lesson examines the main sources of crime data, the patterns they reveal and their significant limitations.

Key Fact

The three main sources of crime data in England and Wales are: (1) police-recorded crime, (2) the Crime Survey for England and Wales (a large-scale victim survey), and (3) self-report studies. Each source captures different dimensions of crime and each has distinct strengths and limitations.

Police-Recorded Crime

Police-recorded crime refers to incidents that are reported to the police and recorded as crimes in their official statistics, published by the Home Office. This source has the longest historical run of data and allows analysis of trends over decades.

However, police-recorded crime has well-documented limitations. First, it only captures crimes that are reported to the police by victims or witnesses. Many crimes — particularly domestic violence, sexual offences, many thefts and hate crimes — are never reported. Second, even among reported crimes, the police have discretion about whether to record an incident as a crime: policing priorities, officer judgements and administrative recording practices all influence what enters the official figures. Third, changes in recording practices over time make comparisons difficult — a rise in recorded sexual offences, for example, may reflect increased willingness to report rather than increased incidence.

From a Marxist perspective, police-recorded statistics reflect the priorities and interests of those with power to define and enforce the law. Crimes committed by the powerful (corporate fraud, tax evasion, health and safety offences) receive less police attention and thus less recording, while street crime committed by the poorest groups is disproportionately pursued. The official statistics therefore tell us as much about policing choices as about crime.

The Crime Survey for England and Wales

The Crime Survey for England and Wales (CSEW) was established in 1982 and asks a large representative sample of households in England and Wales about crimes they have experienced in the previous year, regardless of whether those crimes were reported to the police. By surveying victims directly, it provides a measure of crime that is independent of police recording decisions.

The CSEW consistently records higher crime levels than police-recorded figures because it captures many incidents that go unreported. It is therefore regarded by sociologists as a more comprehensive measure of crime experienced by the population. It also provides consistent data over time unaffected by changes in police recording practices.

The CSEW has its own limitations, however. It relies on self-report by respondents, who may misremember events, under-report sensitive offences (domestic abuse, sexual violence) out of shame or fear, or fail to recognise that an experience constituted a crime. It also excludes crimes against commercial premises, murder (where there is no living victim to survey), and crimes experienced by those living in institutions such as prisons or care homes. Crimes without a direct personal victim — such as drug possession or fraud against organisations — are also outside its scope.

Police-recorded crime: based on reports to the police; affected by policing priorities and recording decisions; shows long-term historical trends; captures crimes against businesses and public property; sensitive to changes in police practice.

Crime Survey for England and Wales: based on victim self-report; independent of policing decisions; more consistent over time; captures unreported crime; excludes murder, victimless crimes, crimes against organisations and under-reporting of sensitive offences.

When the two measures diverge (as they often do), sociologists ask which factors explain the gap. A rise in police-recorded crime during a period of stable CSEW figures, for example, is more likely to reflect improved recording practices than a real rise in offending.

Self-Report Studies

Self-report studies ask individuals to disclose crimes they have committed, often anonymously, providing a third source of data that challenges official crime statistics. Self-report studies have consistently shown that offending is far more widespread across social classes and ethnic groups than official statistics suggest — middle-class and white individuals commit offences at rates much closer to working-class and Black individuals than police-recorded crime implies. This finding supports the interactionist argument that official statistics reflect selective policing and prosecution rather than actual offending behaviour.

Self-report studies have their own limitations: respondents may under-report serious crimes (rape, grievous bodily harm) while over-reporting minor offences; they rely on accurate recall; and they cannot capture offences the respondent does not recognise as crimes or is unwilling to disclose even anonymously.

The Dark Figure of Crime

The dark figure of crime refers to the substantial gap between the amount of crime that actually occurs and the amount that appears in official statistics. This gap exists for two main reasons: crimes are not reported to the police, and crimes that are reported are not always recorded.

Key Fact

Victims may not report crime because: they consider it too trivial; they fear they will not be believed; they are intimidated by the offender; they feel embarrassed or ashamed; they distrust the police; or they resolve the matter informally. Police may not record a reported crime if they judge it insufficiently serious, if the victim withdraws the complaint, or if recording practices are inconsistent.

The dark figure is not evenly distributed across all crime types. Domestic violence and sexual offences have particularly large dark figures because of shame, fear of retaliation and the intimate relationship between victim and perpetrator. Fraud and cybercrime are significantly under-recorded because victims often do not recognise they have been defrauded, report to a bank rather than the police, or assume the police will not act. Minor property crime may go unreported simply because victims feel it is not worth the effort of reporting.

A very common error in sociology exams is to cite official crime statistics as if they were objective facts about the true level of crime in society. The spec is explicit that official statistics have both strengths and weaknesses and that sociological perspectives differ on their usefulness. The dark figure concept is the spec’s core illustration of why official statistics under-represent crime. Always evaluate statistics by asking: what is the source? Who is likely to be missing from this data? What policing or reporting decisions might affect these figures?

Sociological Perspectives on Crime Data

Sociological perspectives disagree about the value and meaning of official crime statistics. Functionalists broadly accept official statistics as a useful measure of crime trends, arguing that they allow governments to monitor social order and direct policing resources. Functionalists treat crime data as a reasonable approximation to reality, while acknowledging recording limitations.

Marxists are far more sceptical. They argue that crime statistics are socially constructed in the interests of the ruling class. The law itself is made by and for the bourgeoisie; enforcement focuses on working-class crime; and the statistics therefore reflect class power rather than objective harm. Official data systematically conceals corporate and white-collar crime while inflating working-class street crime.

Feminist perspectives point out that crime statistics consistently under-represent crimes against women, particularly domestic violence and sexual assault. Patriarchal norms discourage women from reporting these crimes; police response has historically been inadequate; and victim-blaming attitudes in courts further reduce the likelihood of prosecution. Feminists argue that the dark figure of gendered violence is particularly large and that official statistics should always be read critically in this light.

Interactionists argue that crime statistics measure policing activity rather than criminal behaviour. Because the police have discretion about whom to stop, search, arrest and charge, the statistics reflect which groups have been labelled as criminal rather than which groups actually offend more. Self-report studies, which show offending rates that are more evenly spread across social groups, support this critical reading of official data.
source.exam_tip_html: When answering a question about crime statistics, whether short or extended, always distinguish between police-recorded crime and the Crime Survey for England and Wales. Students who write “official statistics show that...” without specifying which source are leaving easy marks on the table. For the 12-mark Discuss question on crime data, the Mastering tier requires you to present at least two contrasting perspectives (for example, functionalist acceptance of official statistics as broadly useful versus Marxist critique of their class bias) and to reach a supported judgement. A strong conclusion might acknowledge that official statistics have genuine utility for identifying trends while also reflecting policing priorities that reproduce social inequality — that both points are true simultaneously is what “how far” questions invite you to argue.
source.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The three main sources of crime data are police-recorded crime, the Crime Survey for England and Wales (a victim survey), and self-report studies. Each captures different dimensions of crime and each has distinct strengths and limitations.
  • The dark figure of crime is the gap between actual crime and officially recorded crime. It exists because many crimes are never reported to the police, and because not all reported crimes are recorded. The dark figure is particularly large for domestic violence, sexual offences and fraud.
  • Sociological perspectives differ on the value of crime statistics: functionalists broadly accept them as useful trend data; Marxists argue they reflect class power and conceal corporate crime; feminists highlight the under-recording of crimes against women; interactionists argue they measure policing activity rather than offending behaviour.
