source.content_html:
Planning Research: Aims, Hypotheses and Pilot Studies

Before collecting a single piece of data, sociologists must make a series of decisions about what they want to find out and how. Research aims define the purpose of a study — for example, “to investigate factors affecting GCSE attainment among students from different socioeconomic backgrounds.” From the aim, the researcher usually develops a hypothesis — a precise, testable prediction, such as “students eligible for free school meals will achieve lower GCSE grades than those who are not.” The hypothesis gives the research direction and allows the findings to be evaluated.

A pilot study is a small-scale test of the research instrument before the main study begins. Imagine a sociologist designing a questionnaire to study attitudes to arranged marriage among young adults in the East Midlands. Running the questionnaire with ten participants first might reveal that a key question is ambiguous, that the response options are too few, or that the time taken is longer than expected. Pilot studies save time and resources by identifying flaws before they contaminate the main data.

Key Fact

The research design process follows a sequence: aim (what do you want to find out?) → hypothesis (what do you predict?) → method choice (how will you gather data?) → sampling (who will you study?) → pilot study (test and refine) → main data collection → analysis.

Sampling: Who to Study?

Sociologists rarely study entire populations. Instead, they select a sample from a sampling frame (a list of the population). The goal is usually a representative sample — one that accurately reflects the characteristics of the wider population, so that findings can be generalised beyond the sample itself.

There are five main sampling methods you need to know:

  • Random sample — every member of the sampling frame has an equal chance of selection. This minimises bias but requires a complete list of the population.
  • Systematic sample — every nth person from the list is selected (e.g. every tenth name). Practical but may introduce bias if the list has a pattern at every nth interval.
  • Stratified sample — the population is divided into groups (strata) by relevant characteristics (e.g. social class, gender) and a proportional number is selected from each stratum. This ensures the sample mirrors the structure of the population.
  • Quota sample — the researcher sets quotas for particular groups (e.g. 50 working-class women, 50 middle-class women) and then selects participants non-randomly until quotas are filled. Quick and inexpensive but non-random, so technically not fully representative.
  • Snowball sample — initial participants recruit others from their networks. Useful for hidden or hard-to-reach populations (e.g. studying drug use, gang membership), but the sample is unlikely to be representative of a wider population.

A sociologist wants to investigate attitudes to higher education among Year 11 students at a comprehensive school in South Yorkshire. The school has 200 Year 11 students. Using a stratified sample, the researcher identifies key strata (e.g. gender, eligibility for free school meals, ethnicity) and selects a proportional number from each group. This increases representativeness — if 30% of students are eligible for free school meals, approximately 30% of the sample will be too, ensuring the findings reflect the full diversity of the year group. A snowball sample would be inappropriate here because students are not a hard-to-reach population and the resulting sample would be biased towards social networks.

Types of Data: Quantitative and Qualitative

Quantitative data takes numerical form — percentages, rates, frequencies, scores. It allows comparisons across large samples, can be analysed statistically, and is associated with approaches that aim for objectivity and replicability. A national survey of 10,000 households can identify patterns and trends in family forms, income or crime rates with a precision no qualitative study can match.

Qualitative data takes verbal form — the words, accounts, feelings and interpretations of research participants. It provides depth and texture, exploring the meanings behind behaviour. An in-depth interview with a family discussing domestic division of labour may reveal nuances about negotiation, resentment and expectation that a tick-box questionnaire would miss entirely.

The choice between quantitative and qualitative approaches often reflects the sociologist’s theoretical perspective. Positivists (associated with functionalism and some Marxist approaches) prefer quantitative data, arguing sociology should emulate natural science. Interpretivists (associated with interactionism) prefer qualitative data, arguing that understanding social behaviour requires grasping the subjective meanings of the participants. In practice, many researchers use mixed methods — combining both types to exploit their complementary strengths.

Primary and Secondary Data; Official Statistics

Primary data is original data collected directly by the researcher. Secondary data is data already gathered by someone else that the researcher re-uses — government statistics, newspaper archives, historical records, published studies.

A very common error is to treat official statistics — figures produced by government departments such as ONS or the Home Office — as straightforward facts. Sociologists are trained to evaluate them critically. Official statistics have strengths: they are large-scale, nationally consistent, free to use, and allow trends to be tracked over time. However, they have important limitations. Crime statistics, for example, only count crimes that are reported to and recorded by the police; the “dark figure” of unreported and unrecorded crime means official figures systematically underestimate the true level of offending. Different perspectives also interpret the same statistics differently: a functionalist might see declining crime rates as evidence of effective social control; a Marxist might argue that statistics reflect selective policing of working-class communities; an interactionist might argue the statistics tell us more about police labelling practices than about actual behaviour. Always evaluate, never just cite.

Key Fact

The five sampling methods are: random, systematic, stratified, quota and snowball. Stratified sampling is best when the researcher wants the sample to mirror the social structure of the population. Snowball sampling is best for hard-to-reach populations where a sampling frame does not exist.
source.exam_tip_html: On a 4-mark Describe about data types or sampling, avoid listing without explaining. A common exam error is to write “quantitative data is numerical and qualitative data is words” and stop there — that is two identifications, not two descriptions. For 4 marks you need to develop each point: explain what makes numerical data useful for sociological research (large-scale, statistically testable, comparable across groups) and what makes qualitative data useful (depth, explores meanings, reveals what statistics miss). Linking to a named method or theoretical perspective (e.g. “positivists prefer quantitative data because…”) lifts the answer further. On the 12-mark Discuss, evaluation of official statistics must be in context — not just “statistics can be wrong” but explaining exactly why the specific statistics are problematic for the research question.
source.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Research design follows a sequence: aim → hypothesis → method → sampling → pilot study → data collection → analysis. Pilot studies test and refine instruments before the main study.
  • Five sampling methods: random (equal chance), systematic (every nth), stratified (proportional by group), quota (non-random quotas) and snowball (for hard-to-reach populations). The aim is a representative sample that allows findings to be generalised.
  • Quantitative data (numbers) suits large-scale pattern-finding; qualitative data (words) suits in-depth meaning. Official statistics are secondary data with both strengths (scale, consistency) and weaknesses (under-reporting, political production) that sociologists must always evaluate critically.

source.content_html:
Applying Methods to Crime and Stratification

Research methods in sociology are not studied in the abstract. For this paper, methods knowledge must be applied to the research contexts of crime and deviance and social stratification. This means being able to explain not just what a method is, but why a particular method is or is not appropriate for researching offenders, the wealthy, the poor, or subcultural groups — and what specific practical and ethical challenges arise in those contexts. A generic list of “advantages and disadvantages of questionnaires” will not earn high marks; the mark scheme rewards contextualised evaluation.

Key Fact

The key methods applied to crime and stratification include: official crime statistics (police-recorded crime), the Crime Survey for England and Wales (a victim survey), self-report studies, ethnographic observation, surveys (as used by Townsend to study poverty), and longitudinal studies (to track life chances over time).

Official Statistics and the Dark Figure

Official crime statistics are produced by the government from crimes recorded by the police. They have been collected in the UK for over 150 years and provide a consistent long-term data source that allows trends to be identified over time. They are a form of secondary data — sociologists analyse figures produced by the police and Home Office rather than collecting them directly.

However, official crime statistics significantly under-represent the actual level of crime through what sociologists call the dark figure of crime. Many crimes are never reported to the police (victims may fear reprisals, not trust the police, consider the crime too minor, or not recognise that they are victims). Others are reported but not recorded. Some crimes — such as domestic violence, sexual assault and corporate crime — are systematically under-represented because of victim reluctance, police discretion and the relative invisibility of white-collar offending. From an interactionist perspective (following Becker), official statistics reflect the outcome of labelling processes — who gets stopped, arrested and convicted — rather than the actual distribution of offending. Marxists argue that official statistics are ideological: they focus attention on street crime (disproportionately associated with the working class) and under-count corporate crime committed by the powerful.

Victim Surveys and Self-Report Studies

The Crime Survey for England and Wales (CSEW) is the major victim survey. It interviews a random sample of around 50,000 households each year, asking respondents whether they have been the victim of any crime in the past twelve months, regardless of whether they reported it to the police. This captures a wider range of offending than official statistics and provides an indication of the dark figure. Sociologists assess its validity as higher than official statistics for crimes such as burglary and vehicle theft, but it still under-represents crimes with no individual victim (corporate crime, drug supply) and crimes where victims are unable or unwilling to disclose (domestic violence, sexual offences, crimes against very young children).

Self-report studies ask participants to anonymously disclose their own offending. They have consistently shown that offending is more evenly distributed across social classes than official statistics suggest — middle-class crime is systematically under-detected and under-prosecuted. This finding challenges the view (implicit in official statistics) that crime is predominantly a working-class problem, supporting the Marxist and interactionist critique of selective enforcement.

Ethnographic research involves the researcher immersing themselves in a social group over a sustained period. Paul Willis’s Learning to Labour (1977) is a key example applied to education and subcultural behaviour. Willis used participant observation and interviews with twelve working-class boys in a Midlands school. His extended engagement with “the lads” produced rich qualitative data about their counter-school culture, their masculine identity and their rejection of educational authority — data that surveys or official statistics could not have captured.

Pat Carlen’s study of women, crime and poverty (1988) used in-depth, unstructured interviews with 39 women who had been convicted of criminal offences. The small, purposive sample allowed Carlen to explore the class and gender dimensions of women’s criminal careers in depth — the class deal and the gender deal that had broken down for each participant. Unstructured interviews generate high-validity qualitative data about individual experiences and motivations, but the small sample size limits generalisability. Both Willis and Carlen illustrate how qualitative methods are particularly valuable for research into marginalised or hard-to-reach groups.

Researching Poverty and Stratification

Townsend’s Poverty in the United Kingdom (1979) illustrates how survey methods can be applied to stratification research. Townsend used questionnaires distributed to over 2,000 households and 6,000 individuals to measure poverty through his deprivation index. The large sample size and standardised questions produced quantitative data with high reliability — the same deprivation index could be applied consistently across all respondents. However, critics questioned whether the absence of certain foods or activities in a household necessarily indicated deprivation or whether it might reflect personal choice or cultural difference, raising questions about validity.

Longitudinal studies track the same individuals over time and are particularly valuable for studying social mobility and life chances. Fiona Devine’s return to Luton to revisit workers first studied by Goldthorpe and Lockwood is an example of a longitudinal research design: by comparing findings at two points in time, she was able to assess whether class experiences had changed. However, longitudinal studies are expensive and face the problem of sample attrition — respondents dropping out over time.

Access: Researching active offenders, gang members or criminal subcultures involves significant access problems. Potential participants may distrust researchers, fear criminal exposure or be geographically dispersed. Snowball sampling — using initial contacts to recruit further participants — is commonly used in this context but produces unrepresentative samples. Researching the very wealthy presents the opposite problem: elite individuals can use social closure and lawyers to restrict access to researchers.

Researcher safety: Fieldwork among violent or criminal groups raises safety concerns. Researchers must weigh the value of participant observation against risks to themselves and their participants. Going covert (not disclosing researcher identity) can improve access but raises serious ethical concerns.

Ethical issues — informed consent: Gaining informed consent from offenders or vulnerable populations requires care. Participants must understand what they are consenting to, but in covert observation this is impossible by definition. Researchers must decide whether the knowledge gained justifies methods that bypass consent — a decision that must be weighed against professional ethical guidelines.

Harm to participants: Research that involves offenders, victims of domestic violence or members of disadvantaged communities may expose participants to harm if they are identified — for example, a gang member whose participation in research becomes known to rivals. Confidentiality and anonymisation of data are essential, but cannot always guarantee complete protection. Researchers also have conflicting obligations if they witness or are told about serious criminal activity.

Researching disadvantaged groups: People experiencing poverty or social exclusion may be harder to reach through standard sampling methods (which often rely on postal addresses or electoral registers that exclude the most marginalised). Townsend’s use of questionnaires distributed across various UK areas addressed some of these problems, but even large-scale surveys can under-sample the homeless or those in temporary accommodation.

Key Fact

Methods evaluation in context is what earns the highest marks. For crime research: state WHY a particular method over- or under-represents a type of crime (e.g. official statistics miss corporate crime because it is rarely reported; victim surveys miss crimes with no individual victim). For stratification research: state WHY Townsend’s questionnaire produced different findings from government poverty statistics, linking method to measurement choice.
source.exam_tip_html: The most common error on methods questions is evaluating a method generically rather than in context. If a question asks you to evaluate the use of official statistics to study crime, the mark scheme rewards points specific to crime research: the dark figure, the problem of unreported crimes, police recording decisions, the ideological critique (focusing on working-class street crime). If asked about studying poverty, the mark scheme looks for reference to Townsend’s deprivation index, the debate between validity and reliability, the difficulty of sampling the most deprived households. On a 12-mark Discuss asking how far official statistics are a useful source of data on crime, present the functionalist view (official statistics reflect real patterns of offending and are reliable over time), the interactionist critique (they reflect labelling and police discretion, not true offending patterns) and the Marxist critique (they focus on working-class crime, under-representing corporate and white-collar offending). Close with a supported judgement.
source.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Official crime statistics are secondary data with high reliability but significant validity problems — the dark figure means they undercount unreported and unrecorded crime. The Crime Survey for England and Wales and self-report studies provide important alternative data sources that capture more of the actual pattern of offending.
  • Ethnographic methods (participant observation and unstructured interviews as used by Willis and Carlen) produce high-validity qualitative data about criminal subcultures and women’s experiences of crime, but face practical problems of access and safety and produce findings with limited generalisability.
  • Researching crime and stratification raises specific practical and ethical challenges: access to offenders, researcher safety, informed consent with vulnerable populations, confidentiality, and the difficulty of sampling the most marginalised groups. Evaluation of methods must always be contextualised to earn the highest marks.

Weakness (up to 2 marks): Respondents may under-report serious or embarrassing offences even when anonymity is guaranteed, reducing validity. Samples are also typically drawn from accessible populations such as school students, missing offenders who have dropped out of education or the most serious, prolific offenders (2 marks).

Ensuring genuinely informed consent requires care — participants must understand the purpose of the research and their right to withdraw without consequences. If a study involves revealing personal financial circumstances or experiences of homelessness or domestic violence, strong anonymisation procedures are essential to protect participants from harm. Townsend addressed this partly through questionnaires that were less intrusive than face-to-face interviews, but even anonymous questionnaire data can carry risks if it can be traced back to individuals.'

Against: dark figure — many crimes are unreported (domestic violence, sexual assault, corporate crime); interactionist critique (Becker) — official statistics reflect labelling and police discretion, not true offending rates; Marxist critique — statistics focus on working-class street crime and under-represent corporate and white-collar crime. Comparison with the Crime Survey for England and Wales (which shows higher crime levels) and self-report studies (showing more distributed offending). A supported judgement on whether official statistics are more useful for understanding trends or for measuring the actual level of crime.

Secure: Both sides present with named sociologists/concepts; judgement offered.

Developing: Relevant but mostly one perspective; some contextualised points; weak conclusion.

Emerging: Basic points; generic methods evaluation; little named sociological theory; minimal evaluation.
